title: From Haider to Strache: how Austria's FPO marched to respectability
text: Austria's far-right Freedom Party (FPO), founded by former Nazis six decades ago, left the political fringes long ago and established itself as a mainstream party, one that could now return to power after a strong showing in Sunday's election. Abroad, the anti-immigration and anti-Islam party is often linked to its former firebrand leader Joerg Haider, who praised Hitler's employment policies. Under Heinz-Christian Strache, however, who has led it since Haider was ousted in 2005, the FPO enjoys broad support in Austria. It topped opinion polls for months until Sebastian Kurz took control of the conservative People's Party in May and carried it to victory in Sunday's parliamentary election. Kurz has yet to name his preferred coalition partner, but the FPO could well end up as kingmaker. The FPO, which helps govern in two provincial and several local governments, says Kurz hijacked its hardline stance on immigration and on curtailing social benefits for foreigners. "One thing is clear: nearly 60 percent of the Austrian population voted for the FPO program," Strache said after winning more than a quarter of the vote, compared with nearly 32 percent for the conservatives, according to projections. The FPO's performance has worried leftist and liberal Austrians, some of Austria's European Union partners, including German Chancellor Angela Merkel, and the World Jewish Congress, although the party today denies being anti-Semitic or anti-EU. "The FPO today is much more radical than it was when it last entered government with the (People's Party) OVP in 2000, but as society as a whole has shifted to the right it is not that obvious," said Andreas Peham, an analyst at the Documentation Center of Austrian Resistance, which researches the far-right.

title: Tajikistan agrees to step up intelligence exchanges with China
text: China's foreign ministry announced on Friday that it had agreed with Tajikistan to set up exchanges of security intelligence, as part of an upgrade in diplomatic relations during a state visit to China by Tajik President Emomali Rahmon. It said both sides will strengthen communications between their defense, security and law enforcement departments and deepen intelligence exchanges. China's plan to rebuild the ancient Silk Road by reconnecting trade routes from its borders into Central and South East Asia, known as the Belt and Road Initiative, has raised new security concerns for the country and its companies. Beijing has worked to deepen security cooperation with countries in Central Asia and elsewhere to compensate for shortfalls in its own intelligence and security measures against terror groups and other threats in the region. The Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a security bloc set up in 2001 by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan to fight radical Islam, has grown to include nearly twenty states as members or partners. In September last year, China agreed to finance and build several outposts for Tajik border guards, along with other facilities, along the porous 1,345-km border between Tajikistan and Afghanistan.

title: Sean Spicer Briefs the Press. Again, No Cameras Allowed.
text: For the country's most prominent political spokesman, Sean Spicer is spending remarkably little time in front of the camera. Monday marked the seventh straight day on which Mr. Spicer, President Trump's press secretary, declined to hold a televised White House press briefing, an unusually long drought for someone whose job is traditionally to be the most visible face of a presidential administration. Instead, Mr. Spicer, who since the inauguration had become a highly rated staple of daytime television, held a session with no cameras allowed, over the objections of the White House Correspondents' Association. The briefing was bound to be contentious. For the first time, Mr. Spicer addressed the explosive and unproven allegations Mr. Trump made over the weekend that his predecessor, Barack Obama, had wiretapped his phones at Trump Tower during the presidential campaign. The public had no way to watch the briefing but could listen to a broadcast by PBS. At one point, when a CNN reporter tried to interject with a question, Mr. Spicer pushed back, saying: “You’re not on camera. You don’t need to jump in.” (He called on the reporter later.) Past press secretaries said it would be unusual for them to stay off television for a full week. And Mr. Spicer's absence from the airwaves comes during a rough stretch: Mr. Trump criticized him in a Fox News interview, and his closest ally in the administration, the chief of staff, Reince Priebus, is under fire from rival factions inside the White House. On Friday, Mr. Spicer was among the group of Mr. Trump's senior aides temporarily banished from Air Force One after Mr. Trump erupted at his staff in frustration during an Oval Office meeting.

Instead, Mr. Spicer, who since the inauguration had become a highly rated staple of daytime television, ran a session with no cameras allowed, over the objections of the White House Correspondents' Association. The briefing was certain to be a heated one. For the first time, Mr. Spicer tackled the explosive and unproven allegations Mr. Trump made over the weekend that his predecessor, Barack Obama, had wiretapped his phones at Trump Tower during the presidential campaign. The public was given no way to watch the briefing but could listen via a broadcast by PBS. At one point, when a CNN reporter tried to jump in with a question, Mr. Spicer snapped back: “You’re not on camera. You don’t need to jump in.” (He called on the reporter later.) On Friday, Mr. Spicer was among the group of Mr. Trump's senior aides temporarily banished from Air Force One after Mr. Trump erupted at his staff in frustration during an Oval Office meeting.

title: U.S. states and Rockefellers push back against U.S. House panel over Exxon climate probes
text: As a number of U.S. states press ahead with investigations into Exxon Mobil Corp's record on climate change, the attorney general of Massachusetts and the Rockefeller family's investment funds told a Congressional committee on Friday that it lacked the power to oversee those probes. The pushback is the newest chapter in a high-stakes battle between the world's largest publicly traded oil company and a coalition of state attorneys general who have said they would pursue Exxon to try to force action on climate change. Last week the House Committee on Science, Space and Technology repeated its demands that state attorneys general hand over any records of consultations the prosecutors held with outside environmental groups before their probes began. Republicans on the committee have said about 20 state officials overreached when they jointly announced in March that they would take part in inquiries into whether Exxon executives misled the public by contradicting research by company scientists that laid out the threats of climate change. State officials have said the committee has no right to get involved. “The Committee lacks authority to interfere with an investigation by the Massachusetts Attorney General’s Office into possible violations of Massachusetts law by ExxonMobil,” said a letter to the committee from the office of Massachusetts Attorney General Maura Healey. title: Pence pushes back Middle East trip in case he is needed for U.S. tax vote

title: U.N. Rights Expert Urges Nations Not to Sign ‘Flawed’ CETA Treaty
text: The trade deal that the European Union and Canada are set to sign is a corporate-driven, fundamentally flawed treaty that should not be signed or ratified without a referendum in each country concerned, a United Nations human rights expert said on 28 October 2016. Alfred de Zayas, the UN Independent Expert on the promotion of a democratic and equitable international order, deplored the pressure placed on the Belgian regional parliament of Wallonia, which initially said it would not approve the treaty but later said its concerns had been met. “A culture of bullying and intimidation becomes apparent when it comes to trade agreements that currently get priority over human rights,” the expert said. In his reports to the Human Rights Council and the General Assembly, Mr. de Zayas has previously warned that CETA is incompatible with the rule of law, democracy and human rights, and he set out how and why before the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe. He believes that both CETA and TTIP, the Trans-Atlantic Trade and Investment Partnership now being negotiated by the EU and the US, give undue power to corporations at the expense of national governments and human rights, and he deplores the fact that the mere existence of investor-state dispute settlement creates a regulatory chill.

title: Nonprofit Work After Retirement? It Might Pay
text: ARCHIE ELAM is making his third career transition. Mr. Elam, now 61 and living in Stamford, Conn., graduated from West Point in 1976. His Army career included serving as head of operations for the 18th Airborne Corps 24th Infantry Division in the first war against Iraq. The Army sent him to earn an M.B.A. at Duke University's Fuqua School of Business, a degree that launched his private sector career in 1996. He worked as a manager at General Electric, United Technologies, Accenture and elsewhere, mostly focused on Six Sigma, a collaborative program for improving company performance by eliminating waste, as well as running customer relations management systems and overseeing other operations. His next act? A job at a nonprofit organization. Mr. Elam recently graduated from Encore! Hartford, a training program for corporate professionals over age 50 who are looking for careers in the nonprofit sector, public agencies and government. “The stuff you volunteer for, you care about, you do for free, and then one day you realize you can get paid to do something you care about,” he said. “How cool is that!” Baby boomers approaching the traditional retirement years often look for purpose and a paycheck in a second career, also called an encore experience, next chapter or unretirement. Whatever it is called, nonprofit work, which focuses on addressing society's pressing needs and promoting arts and culture, holds a particular appeal for many in this group. “People want to give back they want that social impact in the next phase of their life,” said Kate Schaefers, a career and leadership coach in the St. Paul area. “They also turn the retirement stool — Social Security, personal savings and retirement savings — into a stool by adding paid work.” The timing is auspicious.

title: On eve of Gaza reconciliation, Hamas releases Fatah men
text: Hamas released five prisoners from the rival Fatah party on Sunday, and Egypt sent a delegation to the Gaza Strip to oversee the Islamist group's planned handover of administrative control of the Palestinian enclave to a unity government. The West Bank-based Palestinian prime minister, Rami al-Hamdallah, and other officials of the government formed in 2014 are expected in Gaza on Monday to take over ministries and hold a cabinet meeting the following day. Hamas chose reconciliation with the Fatah movement of Western-backed Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas because it is short of money and friends a decade after it seized the enclave in a brief civil war. "We are determined to ... bury the chapter of division so that the homeland can be reunited," Hamdallah said in public remarks in the West Bank city of Ramallah. One cabinet member, Culture Minister Ehab Bseisso, arrived in Gaza on Sunday and, after taking up his post, met deputies and employees. Hamas made its dramatic turn toward reconciliation on Sept. 17, after Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates imposed an economic boycott on the movement's main donor, Qatar, over its alleged support of terrorists. Abbas, whose popularity ratings are low, has faced public pressure to settle his differences with Hamas. Hamas's armed wing remains the dominant power in the territory of 2 million people, which is partially blockaded by Israel and Egypt, citing security concerns for their border restrictions. On the eve of the handover, Hamas freed five Fatah security men it had jailed two years ago for what an Interior Ministry spokesman called "actions harmful to internal security". Their sentences ranged from seven to 15 years.

title: Justice Dept. team studies national security threats posed by internet-connected devices
text: The U.S. Justice Department has set up a threat analysis team to examine potential national security challenges posed by self-driving cars, medical devices and other Internet-connected tools, a senior official said. The new group aims to protect the so-called “internet of things” from exploitation by “terrorist threats” and by others who might try to hack devices to cause loss of life or to achieve political or economic gain, according to Assistant Attorney General John Carlin, who heads the Justice Department's national security division. The team, which has been informally active for about six months, grew out of an understanding that the internet is vulnerable to cyber attacks partly because it was not designed with security in mind, Carlin said after announcing the group on Thursday at the Intelligence and National Security Alliance conference in Washington. Carlin said the group, a small team of about five to 10 people, did “not want to be alarmist” about new technologies such as self-driving cars, but wanted to identify and address the security challenges presented by the internet of things before they are exploited. He pointed to the July truck attack in Nice, France, in which 86 people were killed, as an example of how automated driving systems could pose a national security threat if they were hijacked remotely. “The internet on wheels ... clearly is going to present national security risks as this transformation takes place,” Carlin said. Transportation and public health experts say self-driving cars could dramatically cut auto fatalities and injuries, most of which result from human error. Car hacking has become a growing cyber security concern in recent years.

title: Factbox: Trump tax plan hits snags over local tax deduction, 401(k)
text: The rollout of a tax-cut plan backed by U.S. President Donald Trump and senior congressional Republicans was postponed on Wednesday as groups of lawmakers and special interests dug in over key provisions and demanded changes. Below are some of the most contentious issues in the tax debate, which is likely to play out over the coming weeks and months before the plan can win enough support to pass Congress and go to Trump to be signed into law. 401(k). Republicans are considering new limits on how much money Americans can put each year into their 401(k) retirement accounts on a pre-tax basis. Lower limits on tax-free contributions would generate new revenue to help Republicans pay for the tax cuts they have proposed for high-income earners, corporations and wealthy families' inheritances. Taxpayers can currently direct $18,000 of income tax-free into 401(k)s. Republican tax writers first proposed lowering that cap to $2,400, and after pushback the number has been in flux. Firms that manage 401(k) plans, Wall Street firms that execute trades for them and the 54 million Americans who hold 401(k) accounts could be hurt by such a change. Mortgages. Americans who itemize deductions can currently deduct mortgage interest from their incomes. The plan does not propose changing that directly, but it does propose doubling the standard deduction, a separate line on the tax return that determines eligibility for itemizing. Doubling it would mean fewer Americans itemizing, and so fewer deducting mortgage interest. Critics say doubling the standard deduction would turn the mortgage-interest deduction into a benefit only for higher-income taxpayers. The National Association of Home Builders has come out against the Republican plan and proposed a new, non-itemized tax credit for mortgage interest.

title: Bitcoin Tumbles After Hong Kong Exchange Is Hacked
text: The digital currency Bitcoin tumbled on Wednesday after Bitfinex, a Hong Kong-based exchange, said it had been hacked and that funds had been stolen. The exchange said it had suspended trading, deposits and withdrawals while it looked into which users had been affected. Bitcoin's trading value dropped about 20 percent early on Wednesday, Hong Kong time, but had won back about half the loss by early afternoon. Zane Tackett, Bitfinex's director of community and product development, did not immediately respond to requests for comment. But he said in a Reddit posting that 119,756 Bitcoins had been stolen. Before the hacking became public, that many Bitcoins would have been worth about $72 million. With the currency now lower, the figure is closer to $65 million. The exchange, one of the largest in the world, said in a blog post that any outstanding settlements would be made at the pre-hacking price. “As we account for individualized customer losses, we may need to settle open margin positions, associated financing, collateral affected by the breach,” Bitfinex said in the post. It added that customers' losses would be dealt with later. Security breaches of this kind have raised questions about Bitcoin's viability. The most notable case was the 2014 collapse of Mt. Gox, a Tokyo-based exchange, in which hundreds of thousands of Bitcoins were stolen in a heist that experts and law enforcement officials are still trying to unravel. This past June, a hacker stole more than $50 million worth of Ether, another digital currency, from an experimental virtual currency project called the Decentralized Autonomous Organization.

title: The shortest, most powerful explanation of Trump's victory I've ever seen
text: The Democrats' staggeringly piss-poor performance on Tuesday night, which handed Donald Trump his victory, comes down to one word: Turnout. Hillary Clinton would have won if she had focused her message more on appealing to white, working-class voters in rust belt states such as Iowa, Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. As this New York Times map of the 2012 election shows, President Obama won every one of those states in 2012. Obama also won roughly 2.6 million more votes than Hillary Clinton won in 2016. Donald Trump's narrow margin of victory in the Electoral College was possible only because he won all of those rust belt states. There was hardly any enthusiasm for Hillary Clinton when you look at the exit poll results. Analyzing Reuters/Ipsos exit polling, Times writer Sarah Jaffe found several revealing trends that show why Clinton was a poor choice for the Democrats when it came to motivating voters to go to the polls and vote for their party's nominee: 75 percent of respondents agreed “America needs a strong leader to take the country back from the rich and powerful.” Only slightly fewer agreed that “the American economy is rigged to advantage the rich and powerful,” and, perhaps the kicker, 68 percent believed that “traditional parties and politicians don’t care about people like me.” The numbers back up that argument: Clinton's turnout was lower than Obama's in both 2008 and 2012, even though she still won the popular vote this year. However you slice it, Clinton just wasn't enough of a draw to make the difference, especially in key states such as Florida, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, states Obama won in 2012.
